title: Start Here: What You'll Learn and Why
summary: See why Next.js is worth learning after React, what this course covers and in what order, and what you'll be able to build at the end.
intro: Near the end of the React course, you rendered React on the server by hand: a small Node server, hydration, prerendering, and cache headers for a CDN. It worked, and it was a lot of wiring for one page. Next.js is the framework that does that wiring for you, so you spend your time on the shop instead of the plumbing. This first lesson is the map: why Next.js is worth learning, what the course covers and in what order, how each piece helps when you build for the web, and what you'll be able to do at the end. It assumes the web course and the React course, and nothing else.

steps.title: Why Next.js after React
steps.body:
Before you learn a framework, it helps to know what it saves you from. You've already met the problem it solves, near the end of the React course.

## What React leaves to you

React draws the page from your components and keeps it up to date as state changes. That's all it does, on purpose. Everything around it is up to you: which component shows for which URL, where the data comes from, and where the HTML is made.

In the React course you answered those questions yourself. React Router picked a page for each URL. TanStack Query fetched data from the browser. Then, to get real HTML out of the server instead of an empty `div`, you wrote a Node server that called `renderToPipeableStream`, sent the result, and hydrated it with `hydrateRoot`, the step where React attaches your event handlers to HTML that's already on the screen. Prerendering and cache headers for a CDN took more code again. And Server Components, the components that run only on the server, needed a bundler and a router built for them, which you couldn't easily wire up by hand.

## What Next.js is

**Next.js** is a React framework that does that wiring for you. Recall from the web course that a framework calls your code, and you fill in the parts it leaves open. With Next.js, you write React components in files and folders laid out its way, and it gives you:

- A router built from your folders: a file at `app/products/page.tsx` is the page at `/products`.
- A server that renders your components into HTML, at build time, on each request, or a mix of both in one page.
- Server Components by default, so a component can read a database or call an API with a secret key, and none of that code reaches the browser.
- Caching, so data and pages that rarely change aren't made again on every visit.
- A bundler, **Turbopack**, plus tools for images, fonts, and the tags search engines read.

It's made by Vercel, a company that also sells hosting for it, but it's open source and runs anywhere Node.js runs: your laptop, a server you rent, a Docker container, or a hosting platform.

## What changes when you build with it

The biggest change is where your code runs. In the React course, every component ran in the browser. In Next.js, most components run on the server and send finished HTML, and only the parts that need clicks, typing, or state are sent to the browser as JavaScript. Pages show up fast, search engines and link previews see real content, and the browser downloads less code.

The other change is that one project holds both sides. The page, the code that reads the data, and the code that handles a form all sit in the same folder, written in the same language. You'll still call the Trailhead API, the shop's API you met in the React course, but from the server.

The two examples below show the same product list, first the way the React course built it and then the way this course will.

examples.title: A product list in the React course
examples.prompt: A page from a single-page app: it runs in the browser, so it fetches the products after it loads and shows a loading message until they arrive.
examples.explanation: The browser downloads the app's JavaScript first, then runs this component, which asks TanStack Query for the products. Only then does the request leave for the API, and only when its answer arrives does the list appear. Until that moment, the page shows Loading products…, and that's what a search engine that doesn't run JavaScript sees too. This is client-side rendering, CSR, from the React course. It's a fine fit for a dashboard behind a login, and a slow first visit for a shop.

examples.title: The same list in Next.js
examples.prompt: The page at `app/products/page.tsx` in a Next.js project. It's a Server Component, so it runs on the server, and `listProducts` is a small function from the project's `lib` folder that calls the API.
examples.explanation: The component is `async`, so it can simply `await` the data. There's no hook, no loading flag, and no effect, because it runs on the server before any HTML is sent. The browser receives a finished list in the very first response. The file's place in the project, `app/products`, is what makes it the page at `/products`, with no router setup. And none of this code is sent to the browser, since nothing in it needs to run there. The `@/` at the start of the import means the project's root folder. The lessons ahead explain each piece: where this runs, how `listProducts` is cached so the page isn't rebuilt on every visit, and what to show while slow data is on its way.

steps.title: The path through the course
steps.body:
Next.js has a lot of features, and they make the most sense in a certain order. A few ideas from the first lessons, like where a component runs, come back in every lesson after them. So here's the whole path, and why each stop comes where it does.

```diagram start-here-path
Each stop builds on the ones before it, so take them in order.
```

## 1. From React to Next.js

You start by creating a Next.js project, learning what each of its files does, and following one request from the address bar to a finished page. Then you learn the router: how folders become URLs, how layouts wrap pages, and how to show a loading state, an error, or a 404 page. Last comes the idea everything else rests on: **Server Components** and **Client Components**, which decide where each part of your page runs. Most mistakes people make in Next.js come from mixing those two up, so the course spends a whole lesson on them.

## 2. Data and rendering

Next, the data. You'll fetch it on the server, run requests side by side instead of one after another, and let slow parts of a page arrive later while the rest shows at once, which is called **streaming**. Then **caching**: keeping a result so the next visitor doesn't wait for it again, and clearing it when the data changes. Last, the rendering modes you compared in the React course, CSR, SSR, SSG, and ISR, mapped onto real Next.js pages, so you can choose one for each page and check what you got.

## 3. Mutations and the server

A **mutation** is any change to data: adding to a cart, posting a review, logging in. You'll handle forms with **Server Actions**, functions that run on the server when a form is sent. You'll write **Route Handlers**, which answer HTTP requests the way an API does, and **proxy**, code that runs before every request. Then you'll keep secrets on the server, check who's logged in, and protect every page and action that needs it.

## 4. Shipping

Then you get the app ready for other people: page titles and previews for search engines and shared links, images that load at the right size, fonts that don't make the page jump, and scripts from other companies that don't slow it down. After that you build it for production and deploy it, either to a hosting platform or to a server of your own with Docker.

## 5. Testing

Last, you test it. Some parts of a Next.js app are plain functions and components you can test quickly with Vitest, the way you did in the React course. Server Components are best tested through a real browser against a real build, with Playwright. You'll also learn to fake the API the server calls, which takes a different trick than faking one the browser calls.

## Why this order

Each stop leans on the ones before it. Caching makes no sense until you know what runs on the server. Server Actions build on caching, since after a write you tell the cache what changed. And tests come last, because you can only test what you know how to build.

steps.title: How you'll work through it
steps.body:
The course works the way the React course did, with one shop you build up lesson by lesson. Knowing what's in it and what you'll need saves you guessing later.

## The shop you'll build

The example app is **Trailhead**, a small store for outdoor gear: twelve products in four categories (packs, tents, apparel, and cooking), a product page for each, a cart, and an account page. Prices are whole numbers of cents, so `34900` is $349.00. Two products are out of stock, and one has no reviews yet, so the pages have real edge cases to handle.

Its data comes from the **Trailhead API**, the same small shop API the React course called. It's a small server that runs on your computer, from a `trailhead-api` folder in your Playground, and answers at `http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1`. The routing lesson adds it, where the shop first needs it. Started with `TRAILHEAD_DELAYS=1`, it answers after short delays, like a real API across a network, so you can watch loading states and streaming happen. This time your Next.js server calls it, not the browser.

Each shop page needs something different. The about page never changes, product pages change now and then, stock changes all the time, and the cart belongs to one person. Those differences are what the rendering and caching lessons are about.

## What you need

- **Node.js 20.9 or newer.** Next.js runs on it. Check with `node --version`. The lessons ran on Node 24.
- **Next.js 16.4 or newer, with React 19.3.** The first real lesson creates a project with them, and npm downloads both.
- **A terminal and a browser.** Use the Playground's terminal, or your computer's own, the way you did in earlier courses. A Next.js server keeps one terminal busy while it runs, so you'll often want a second one for commands.
- **DevTools.** The Network panel is where you'll watch pages stream and navigations fetch data.

## The docs come with Next.js

Every Next.js project has the full documentation for its exact version inside `node_modules/next/dist/docs`, as Markdown files you can read in your editor. The project even includes a file called `AGENTS.md` that tells AI coding tools to read them, because Next.js changes quickly and older advice is often wrong. That goes for advice from people too. When a blog post and the bundled docs disagree, trust the docs that came with your version.

## How the lessons read

The lessons work like the ones in the React course. Each part opens on why its idea matters, then shows how it works. Code says which file it lives in, like `app/products/[slug]/page.tsx`, and output is always real, copied from an actual run, so your times, ports, and file names may differ a little. Diagrams draw the parts that are easier to see than to read, like a request crossing from the browser to the server and back.

## What you'll be able to do

By the end of the course, you'll be able to:

- Create a Next.js project and explain what every file and folder in it does.
- Lay out pages, layouts, loading states, and error pages with the App Router.
- Decide which components run on the server and which in the browser, and pass data between them safely.
- Fetch data on the server, stream the slow parts, and cache what doesn't change.
- Pick a rendering mode for each page, and read the build's report to check it.
- Handle forms with Server Actions, protect pages and actions, and keep secrets on the server.
- Ship it to a platform or your own server, and test it with Vitest and Playwright.

The next lesson starts by creating the project.

recap:
- Next.js is a React framework: it adds a router built from folders, server rendering, caching, and a bundler, so you don't wire them by hand.
- Most components run on the server and send HTML, and only the interactive parts ship JavaScript to the browser.
- The course goes in order: from React to Next.js, data and rendering, mutations and the server, shipping, then testing.
- The example app is Trailhead, a gear shop whose server calls the Trailhead API on your computer.
- You need Node.js 20.9 or newer, a terminal, and a browser with DevTools.
- Every project ships its own docs in node_modules/next/dist/docs, and they win when other advice disagrees.
